matching.reasoningTemplate: Sharp pleuritic chest pain relieved by sitting forward, with typical ECG changes, suggests pericarditis.

harrison.pages: Harrison 22e p.90 (PE summary box); p.102 (tamponade as cause of shock); p.145-150 (Chest Discomfort: pericardial pain, exam, ECG); p.312 (dyspnea/pericardial disease table); p.324 (uraemic friction rub)
clinicalPearls: Diagnosis rests on the combination of characteristic chest pain, a pericardial friction rub, and characteristic ECG changes; echocardiography can be normal in roughly a third to half of cases, so a normal echo does not exclude pericarditis (p.90).
The pericardial pain is typically pleuritic and positional: worse supine and on inspiration/coughing, relieved by sitting up and leaning forward (p.146, p.149).
Pain referred to the trapezius ridge is characteristic of pericardial inflammation and is not typical of angina (p.149).

Most of the pericardium is insensitive to pain; the discomfort of pericarditis is thought to arise largely from accompanying pleural inflammation, explaining its pleuritic, positional quality and referral to shoulder/neck (p.147).
A pericardial friction rub on auscultation reflects pericardial inflammation and is a key physical sign (p.149).
Pericarditis is an uncommon final diagnosis among undifferentiated acute chest pain presentations (about 4% in one ED series), so other causes are statistically more likely (p.145).
harrison.pathophysiology: Inflammation of the pericardium from infectious or noninfectious causes. Because the visceral and most of the parietal pericardium are insensitive to pain, the discomfort is attributed mainly to associated pleural inflammation, producing pleuritic, position-dependent pain that, via overlapping phrenic and C3-C5 somatic innervation, may be referred to the shoulder, neck, and trapezius ridge (p.147, p.149).
infectionMimics: Acute myocarditis (often viral; chest discomfort and ST/T-wave changes can overlap)
nonInfectiousMimics: Acute coronary syndrome / STEMI (diffuse ST elevation of pericarditis can be mistaken for infarction)
Takotsubo (stress) cardiomyopathy (ST elevation and biomarker rise mimicking MI)
Aortic dissection extending into the pericardium
additionalInvestigations: 12-lead ECG looking for diffuse ST-segment elevation with PR-segment depression (p.149)
Chest radiograph (pericardial calcification suggests chronic pericarditis; usually unremarkable in acute disease) (p.150)
Echocardiography to detect effusion (may be normal in 34-50% of acute cases) (p.90)
Measurement of pulsus paradoxus when tamponade is suspected (p.312)
redFlags: Hypotension with significant tachycardia, suggesting tamponade and haemodynamic compromise (pericarditis with tamponade is a high-risk, potentially life-threatening cause of chest pain) (p.147, p.150)
Abnormal jugular venous pulse pattern consistent with pericardial tamponade (p.149)
Tamponade is a recognised cause of obstructive shock (p.102)
pitfalls: Diffuse (multi-lead) ST-segment elevation not confined to a single coronary territory, together with PR-segment depression, helps distinguish pericarditis from acute MI; ascribing these ECG changes to ischaemia is a key pitfall (p.149).
A normal echocardiogram does not exclude pericarditis (effusion absent in 34-50%) (p.90).
Chest-wall tenderness does not exclude myocardial ischaemia, and an unremarkable physical exam is not reassuring (p.149).
Low-grade fever is nonspecific and can accompany MI and thromboembolism as well as pericardial inflammation (p.149).
